<reason>PRO anchored the debate on "presumptively" as a rebuttable default and an error-asymmetry frame, then defended it concretely: the compelled-firm pressure question was answered with specific rebuttal structures (trustee control, non-controlling stakes, divest-on-trigger), and the "stalled pit" objection was answered with the plausible Japan/Australia post-2010 example plus the point that peacetime volume from rival-controlled assets is exactly what vanishes under coercion. PRO's closing move—that CON's own list of blocking facts and existing mitigation tools concedes every component and disputes only who proposes them first—narrowed the clash effectively. CON built a genuinely strong case (midstream, not title, is the chokepoint; host licenses govern flows; blocking doesn't build separators; capital deterrence) and gave a credible answer to PRO's fork (title decides financing but not redirection of licensed ore) and to the jurisdiction point (screening listed bids isn't truck-stopping power). But CON's decisive empirical premise—that allied capital simply will not appear—was asserted rather than supported, while PRO's clipped first rebuttal is a real execution cost. On balance PRO made the decision rule clearer and left CON arguing the price of the default rather than defeating the asymmetry.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A4.6–4.7 fork—CON cannot both claim title is irrelevant to where ore flows and that losing the rival bidder kills the mine—combined with the observation that state acquirers pay premiums because they know which is true. CON's reply in B4.4 (title finances the pit but cannot redirect licensed ore) was the sharpest defensive move of the debate, but it conceded that ownership matters enough to control whether supply exists at all, which fed PRO's leverage story.</best_rebuttal>
